newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler idles more workers as a result of strike.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler idles more workers as a result of strike.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. idled nearly 1,700 more workers Tuesday as a result of a six-day-old engine plant strike that has halted production of its hot-selling Ram pickup trucks and Jeep Grand Cherokee sport utility vehicles.

Meanwhile, General Motors Corp., already dealing with a 12-day-old walkout at its Oklahoma City car plant, received a new strike deadline from the United Auto Workers union, this time at its Pontiac, Mich., assembly plant.

New facilities affected by the Chrysler engine plant strike include the Conner Avenue Assembly Plant in Detroit that produces the Viper sports car. Chrysler has now told more than 13,700 workers to stay home as a result of the strike.

About 1,800 members of United Auto Workers union Local 51 walked off their jobs at the Mound Road Engine Plant in Detroit early April 10. Union leaders are demanding that Chrysler address alleged discrimination issues and stop plans to outsource work that would cost about 200 jobs.

The strike has choked off Chrysler's only source of V-6, V-8 and V-10 truck engines. It is the first time in more than 20 years a labour stoppage has forced such a widespread production shutdown at Chrysler.
Chrysler spokesman Tony Cervone said Tuesday another 100 to 150 workers may be sent home from various plants later this week because of the strike.

GM's labour headaches also grew Tuesday when it received a "five-day" strike notice from the UAW for its Pontiac East full-size pickup truck assembly plant in Pontiac, Mich. About 5,400 UAW members from Local 594 could walk off the job at 11:59 p.m. (EDT) April 22 if a new contract is not reached.
The facility produces full-size GMC and Chevrolet C/K pickup trucks, as well as chassis cab trucks.

GM spokesman Daniel Flores said the company hopes it can reach a new agreement without a work stoppage. UAW officials said the two sides have been unable to agree on a variety of manpower issues, such as work that GM wants to subcontract, and line-speed accelerations.
GM also is trying to resist UAW demands for increased manpower at Oklahoma City and some 30 other facilities that have not reached agreements on new local labour contracts.
GM Chairman John Smith said he saw no easy solutions to the local talks, because GM needs agreements that "make business sense."
"We'll have problems from time to time. I don't see any way around it," he told reporters at a breakfast meeting.
He said the union's Detroit leadership recognises the need for GM to improve its assembly efficiency, but "can't strong-arm the locals" into accepting job cuts.

Cervone at Chrysler said senior negotiators from both sides have held telephone discussions on smaller issues relating to the walkout. He predicted formal "main table" talks would resume Wednesday. The two sides have not held substantive talks since the strike began.
Local 51 President Sam Nardicchio remained steadfast Tuesday that workers who sacrificed during Chrysler's lean years be able to enjoy the company's profitable times.

"We gave up a lot of money in the '80s to save this corporation. Now we're making record profits," he said. "When you're making a billion a quarter, nobody can understand why they want to continue giving jobs away."
Last Thursday, Chrysler posted first quarter profits of $1.029 billion, up 2.4 percent from a year ago.

New plants and employees affected by the strike were: 1,200 of the 2,500 workers at the Warren Stamping plant in Warren, Mich.; 350 workers out of 1,600 at the Dayton Thermal Products Plant in Dayton, Ohio; 30 out of 600 workers at Ajax Trim in Ajax, Ontario; and about 100 workers at the Conner Avenue Assembly.

The company already had suspended production at four plants in Michigan, Missouri and Windsor, Ontario, that produce the Ram full-size pickup truck, Dakota compact pickup truck; Jeep Grand Cherokee; and full-size vans.

Meantime, the strike is also affecting suppliers. Lear Corp. spokeswoman Leslie Touma said the company has sent home about 350 workers at two plants that serve Chrysler light truck assembly operations in Detroit and St. Louis.
